instruments.evidence: 20 files. Boundaries: Go service->handler (new OmniChatSpeech result type); handler->browser (new GET /omnichat/conversations/:id/call-speech/:turn/:sequence); Go->Redis (call sentence keys); Go->websocket->browser (two new message types); Go->OpenRouter (a real streaming callback where the callback was previously discarded); browser->Go (turn and sequence as URL parameters).

Read 13 prior ledgers. voice-R1 (a per-sentence route behind a per-call rate limiter) is the same shape as the new route and was guarded before this review by giving it its own budget. cache-R3 (authenticatedFetch defaults to cache no-store) and pragma-R1 (the API middleware stamps Pragma/Expires) both bear on the new route's headers and agree with the private,no-store it sets. stream-R1 (cross-origin credentials) is satisfied by authenticatedFetch. call-R1-blind: control tests must pass standalone, so both new vitest tests configure every mock in their own body.

Printed the real artifact -- the sequence of sentences she speaks -- for 16 materially different token streams, at chunk sizes 2,3,4,6,7 and 10000 (one-shot). Found R1, R2 and R3. Re-printed after the fix: short openers stand alone, Mr./J. R. stay whole, 3.5 stays one number, narration is stripped and never split, and the overlong break lands on a word.

OmniChatCallModal's markup is unchanged; only the turn logic changed. Confirmed the two status values the new code sets, 'speaking' and 'ready', are both rendered (the pulse animation and the disabled mic button at OmniChatCallModal.tsx:649 and :749) rather than invented.

Printed status, every header and the body for the new route across 8 inputs: a real sentence (200 audio/wav, private no-store, nosniff, correct Content-Length), a narration-only sentence (204, no body), an expired turn (404), a path-traversal turn (404 at the router), a Redis wildcard turn (400), sequence 0, -1 and an overflowing sequence (400). Also printed GetMessageSpeech for the fresh, cached and lost-the-upsert paths: identical header shape, correct bytes and length on each.

One new query, GetConversationVoiceOwned. Read it against the sibling it replaces: it decides ownership and voice in one statement, keeping the archived_at, is_active and owner/visibility predicates the live-call context query already used. No migration.
Both websocket type strings and all four payload keys grepped on both sides and matched exactly: omnichat_call_sentence and omnichat_call_sentences_done; conversation_id, turn, sequence, spoken.

The field the browser reads is the field the server sets, verified by printing both HTTP paths and by the key match above. OmniChatSpeech.Fresh is set in generateSpeech and read in the handler; the round trip is asserted in omnichat_voice_test.go.

SpokenText runs in the splitter and again in SpeakSentence. It is idempotent and the two are separated by Redis, so this is defence across a boundary rather than drift. The narration rule itself lives in one place, narrationIsOpen.

The provider genuinely streams -- processStreamWithTelemetry calls onChunk per SSE delta -- so the call path now receives real tokens where the contract layer previously passed func(string){}. Generation is bounded at 25s (personalGenerationTimeout), comfortably inside the browser player's 45s give-up, so the server can never still be emitting sentences for a turn the browser has abandoned.
OmniChatSpeech.Fresh crosses a boundary but is a plain Go struct field, not a hand-written decoder or column list. Traced it from generateSpeech through the singleflight result to the handler write.

Broke the reader rather than the writer: printed the handler's response for a result carrying Fresh and for one without, and confirmed the fresh path serves the fresh bytes with a matching Content-Length rather than silently falling through to storage.

The fixtures mint values the way production does: the sentence tests push text in small chunks the way the provider streams it rather than whole sentences, and the turn identifier in the handler probes is a real UUID because that is what uuid.NewString produces and what ValidCallTurn requires.

Real inputs pass: ordinary replies, quoted speech, ellipses, decimals, abbreviations, initials, stage directions and one-shot non-streamed replies all produce the right sentences; a real UUID turn returns audio.

Hostile inputs are refused: a Redis wildcard turn and a path-traversal turn never reach the key builder, and the sentence route asks by number so it can never be made to synthesise client-supplied text.

Boundaries probed: empty pending, sequence 0, -1, and a value that overflows Atoi; a sentence longer than the store cap is truncated; a reply with no terminator at all is still spoken; a reply that is only narration produces nothing.

Compared with the two siblings. GetMessageSpeech validates content type and size -- the new route gets the same protection through validOmniChatSpeechAudio inside SpeakSentence, which enforces both. TranscribeCallTurn's active-call ownership check has no counterpart, but the new route grants no capability without one, because a sentence only exists in Redis if a call produced it.

The buffered contract loop is now unreachable for calls, deliberately and documented. Every other branch stays reachable: the whole-reply speech still runs when no sentence was spoken, when the run was cancelled, and on every non-call message.

Sentence and Done failures are logged with conversation_id and sequence. A cache write that fails returns before announcing, so the browser is never told to fetch something that was not stored. A fetch the browser cannot complete degrades to the whole-reply voice, which reports its own failure on screen.

Checked every generation path is wired: NewChatbotService is constructed once, in cmd/server, and the reply scheduler shares that instance, so no binary generates replies without the sentence sink. cmd/worker builds no ChatbotService.

maxSpokenSentenceRunes (320, the splitter) and maxCallSentenceRunes (600, the store) are two bounds on the same value, kept because the store does not trust its caller and the second can never fire given the first. No other constant is duplicated.

The shape behind R1-R3 is a splitter deciding a boundary from a length rather than from content. Grepped every other place this repository splits prose: splitDeliverableMessages cuts on blank lines, not terminators, so it carries neither the abbreviation nor the mid-word defect.
Found R4. The sentence run is started at the top of the turn to overlap synthesis with generation, while the avatar decision is made after the reply arrives.

sentenceStream is touched only from the goroutine that runs generation: onChunk is invoked synchronously inside GenerateWithOptions, and flush/stop run after it returns. The browser player is single-threaded and guards re-entry with a pumping flag.

A turn that fails half way calls stop() and announces Done with the count actually produced, so the caller hears what was already said and no more; the user-facing error is still persisted and delivered as the message, and is not spoken over the top.

Sentences are the only thing persisted and they expire on their own after three minutes, so a caller who hangs up mid-reply leaves nothing behind. No object storage is written on the call path at all, which is one of the three latency fixes.

Two control patches built and replayed by hand. sentence-boundary.patch restores the buffer-length rule and produces three real assertion failures showing exactly the defects ("Hey. I missed you today." as one sentence, "I went to see Mr." split, and "...aaa ext" cut mid-word). video-double-voice.patch produces "Number of calls: 1" against a not.toHaveBeenCalled assertion. Both build cleanly with the fix reverted, so each fails as a test rather than as a compile error. Artifact re-printed after restoring.

UNVERIFIED, and recorded as such rather than buried. The sentence splitter's output has never been through a real synthesiser or a real call: every sentence above was printed, not heard. findings.summary: a minimum sentence length glued every short opener to the sentence after it, so "Hey. I missed you today." was one utterance and her first word waited for the whole reply -- which is the delay the feature exists to remove

findings.summary: a full stop after an abbreviation ended a sentence, so "I went to see Mr. Yang about the roof." was spoken as "I went to see Mister." and then "Yang about the roof." -- the length minimum hid this rather than fixing it, because it measured the buffer instead of looking at the word
